Mapping pluvial flood susceptibility in Lisbon’s Baixa Pombalina

A GIS model that scores how readily each 10 m cell of central Lisbon could collect rainwater, followed by experiments in showing that result in 3D. It ranks places relative to each other. It does not predict flood depth.

Lower susceptibilityHigher
Context
Master’s project in GIS and Science, NOVA IMS, 2026
Tools
ArcGIS Pro, Unreal Engine, Cesium for Unreal
Data
DGT terrain model (50 cm), Copernicus Imperviousness Density 2024 (10 m), Lisbon City Council building footprints

The question

Baixa Pombalina is low-lying, densely built and has a history of flooding. When heavy rain exceeds what the drains can carry, water collects in streets and squares. This project asks where terrain and surface conditions make that more likely, and whether 3D views help explain the answer to people who don’t read maps for a living.

Three criteria, one scale

Each criterion was resampled to a common 10 m grid and rescaled to 0–1, so they could be combined without sorting them into arbitrary classes first.

CriterionHow it was builtRescaled as
SlopeFrom the 2 m terrain model, averaged over 5 × 5 cellsFuzzy “small” membership: flatter ground scores higher (0.25–1)
Flow accumulationD8 method on the 2 m terrain model, maximum over 5 × 5 cellsln(x + 1) ÷ ln(942,774), because a few cells dominate the raw range (0.08–1)
ImperviousnessCopernicus density raster; the 255 “outside coverage” value set to NoDataDivided by 100 (0–1)

Combining them

With equal weights (one third each), the land-only index runs from 0.146 to 0.967, with a mean of 0.671. Dense streets score high, and linear patterns follow the street grid. The slopes around Castelo de São Jorge vary more. The Tagus was clipped out with a hand-drawn boundary, which is approximate.

I haven’t yet compared this map with independently mapped historical flood locations, so it can’t be said to find where flooding has actually happened.

How much do the weights matter?

Drag across the map to compare the equal-weight model with one that gives flow accumulation 50% and slope and imperviousness 25% each.

Flow accumulation 50%Equal weights
Mean difference 0.084
Maximum 0.153
Std. deviation 0.036

The broad pattern holds, but individual cells shift, so the index depends partly on the weights chosen. Only one alternative was tested, which doesn’t establish how robust the model is.

Seeing it in 3D

I built a local scene in ArcGIS Pro from the 50 cm terrain model, with building footprints extruded to an illustrative 15 m. The flood simulation used the 44.5 mm of rain recorded in one hour at the Instituto Geofísico station on 7 December 2022, applied evenly over a 1 m grid. It has no infiltration, evaporation or drainage, so it is not a reconstruction of that event.

Comparing views, 2D was easier for judging spatial patterns, while 3D made the setting easier to grasp, especially for non-specialists. Buildings can also hide the water they surround.

Unreal Engine

I exported the flood raster to Unreal Engine and placed it in a Cesium 3D model of Praça do Comércio. Because the raster covers the whole area, water also appears on roofs, which is unrealistic and a limit of this method. The street-level view uses a 40 cm water depth chosen for illustration only.

Limitations

  • The terrain model covers a limited area, so some upstream contributing ground may be missing.
  • The 10 m grid generalises small features that steer water.
  • Results rest on chosen normalisation methods and weights, with one alternative tested and no validation against observed floods.
  • Drainage networks, rainfall variability, soil infiltration and tides aren’t modelled.
  • The 3D scenes use simplified buildings and rainfall, and the Unreal visuals are illustrative.

Conclusion

GIS multi-criteria evaluation can show relative pluvial susceptibility in a dense city, and 3D views can make flood information more intuitive. Neither should be read as a prediction. Next steps are drainage data, historical flood observations and hydraulic modelling.

Use of AI: I used Claude and ChatGPT to find data sources, get guidance on ArcGIS Pro procedures and talk through GIS concepts. The processing, analysis, maps, 3D work and conclusions are my own.
